summary: A modular monolith build: React SPA on the frontend, Go for the backend, PostgreSQL for data, hosted on Fly.io for about $1,190-2,792 a month. It plans for GDPR, builds on the team's Go, pushes live updates, and ships as one deployable that a team of 5 can build in 12 weeks.

frontend.justification: React SPA (Vite) is the frontend for a Realtime chat / collaboration / multiplayer project with about 10,000 daily users (~521 requests/s at peak), built by a team of 5 in 12 weeks. Search visibility is marked not needed (behind login), so rendering in the browser is acceptable, and it scores 5.0/5 for rich, app-like interaction. Next.js (React) is within 0.7 stack points, inside the tie margin (stacks this close count as tied); the tie went to React SPA (Vite) on lower vendor lock-in (5 vs 6, summed lock-in).

alternatives.why_not: Within the 1-point tie margin (counted as tied): swapped in, its stack scores 0.7 points lower; either is defensible. React SPA (Vite) is stronger on low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0), learning curve (4.0 vs 3.0); Next.js (React) is stronger on performance / latency (4.0 vs 3.0), development speed (5.0 vs 4.0); Next.js (React) takes a penalty: No search visibility needed: server rendering adds a Node.js server for pages that React SPA (Vite) serves as static files.
Ruled out: Mobile toolkit; web is a target, so the primary frontend is a web framework (mobile app suggested as companion)

backend.justification: Go (net/http, chi or Gin) serves the API at about 521 requests/s at peak (Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once)) for a team of 5. The team lists Go, so it needs no new server language (team skill match 4.5/5). It runs as a long-running Go service, so background jobs, WebSockets and database connection pools live in one deployable process. Realtime is core, and it scores 4.0/5 on realtime fit. It leads the runner-up, Elixir + Phoenix, by 3.1 stack points (points of the overall stack score, the average of the four layer scores).

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.1 points. Go (net/http, chi or Gin) is stronger on team skill match (4.5 vs 1.5), learning curve (5.0 vs 2.0); Elixir + Phoenix is stronger on realtime fit (5.0 vs 4.0), development speed (4.0 vs 3.0); Elixir + Phoenix takes a penalty: Nobody on the team listed Elixir or a closely related skill: a new server language to learn.

database.justification: Your data is mainly relational and reaches about 200 GB within 12 months; PostgreSQL fits relational data 5/5. Strong consistency is assumed, since no input says stale reads are acceptable, and PostgreSQL gives it: a read after a write always sees that write. The workload is write-heavy, and its write scaling scores 3/5. Its share of the estimated bill is $600-$1,244 a month, against a total budget of $1,500 a month. It leads the runner-up, Microsoft SQL Server, by 2.1 stack points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 2.1 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0), portability (low lock-in) (5.0 vs 3.0).

Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.1 points. PostgreSQL is stronger on realtime fit (3.0 vs 2.0); MySQL takes a penalty: Customers share one database and in MySQL privileges stop at table and column level, so the tenant filter lives in every application query.

hosting.justification: Fly.io hosts the stack for users in regions you did not state at a 99.9% availability target. It runs the Go API as long-running processes with WebSockets, sized for ~521 requests/s at peak. Its share of the estimated bill is $375-$845 a month, against a total budget of $1,500 a month. It leads the runner-up, Google Cloud Run, by 3.1 stack points.

alternatives.why_not: Swapping it in lowers the stack score by 3.1 points. Fly.io is stronger on realtime fit (5.0 vs 3.0), performance / latency (5.0 vs 4.0); Google Cloud Run is stronger on scalability (5.0 vs 4.0), low ops burden (5.0 vs 4.0).

Request-scoped functions either cannot hold a WebSocket (Lambda behind a function URL, Netlify) or hold each one as a running function pinned to one instance (Vercel beta), so broadcasting to all of them needs a separate pub/sub or realtime service.

supporting.justification: Read-heavy traffic, a tight latency target or hot key-value data: keep hot reads and sessions in memory in front of a durable primary database. The 100 ms p95 target (requirements.p95_latency_ms) leaves little time for repeated database reads.

alternatives.choice: The database's own buffer cache only
alternatives.why_not: It holds hot rows only until the working set outgrows the database's memory, and every read still costs a database round trip

tradeoffs: Cached data can be stale: each write must expire or update the keys it changes

supporting.choice: Redis pub/sub for cross-instance fan-out (Upstash Redis on Fly)
supporting.justification: With several app instances, a message published on one must reach sockets on all others. Up to 5,000 users online at once (scale.peak_concurrent_users) hold open connections.

alternatives.choice: Polling the API every few seconds
alternatives.why_not: Every client asks again and again, which multiplies requests and still shows changes late

tradeoffs: Open connections hold memory per user and need pub/sub to reach users on other instances

supporting.choice: Yjs shared documents (CRDTs) synced over the WebSocket connection, with Hocuspocus or y-websocket as the sync server
supporting.justification: Many people editing one document at once need conflict-free merging; CRDTs merge concurrent edits without locks, and the server stores snapshots, not every stroke. Sized for the 50,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: A central server must order every edit, and offline edits merge less cleanly than with CRDTs

tradeoffs: Document snapshots grow with edit history and need compaction

supporting.justification: Send emails, process uploads and call slow APIs outside the request path. Sized for the 50,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Doing the work inside the web request
alternatives.why_not: Slow emails, uploads and API calls would hold the request open and fail with it

tradeoffs: A job can run twice after a retry, so handlers must be idempotent

supporting.justification: Uploaded files and video belong in object storage, not the database. The scenario stores 200 GB within 12 months (scale.data_volume_gb_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: They bloat backups and the database disk, which costs several times more per GB than object storage

tradeoffs: Files and their database rows can drift apart: delete or replace both together

supporting.choice: Cloudflare CDN in front of the uploads bucket
supporting.justification: Serve uploads from the CDN, not the app server; resize images on the fly instead of storing every size. Sized for the 50,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.choice: Serving files through the app server
alternatives.why_not: Each download holds an app connection and pays the app host's egress price

tradeoffs: Links that leak can be shared until they expire, so keep their lifetime short

supporting.justification: Card data never touches your servers, which keeps your PCI-DSS audit scope to the smallest self-assessment form (SAQ A). Sized for the 50,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: Suits large merchants with negotiated contracts; more setup than a first release needs

alternatives.choice: Taking card details on your own pages
alternatives.why_not: Card data on your servers moves the PCI-DSS audit from the shortest self-assessment (SAQ A) to a full one

tradeoffs: Every transaction pays the gateway's fee, and refunds and disputes follow its process

supporting.justification: Do not hand-roll password storage, MFA or SSO. Sized for the 50,000 users expected at 12 months (scale.users_12_months).

alternatives.why_not: A server to run, patch and back up, for no feature this project needs
Password storage, MFA, resets and lockouts are easy to get wrong and are the first things attackers test

tradeoffs: Sign-in depends on the identity provider staying up; moving users off it later is a migration

supporting.justification: Traces, metrics and error tracking from day one; required to defend an availability target. A 99.9% availability target (requirements.availability) allows about 43 minutes of downtime a month, so failures must show within minutes.

alternatives.why_not: Without traces and metrics there is no way to see which call is slow or failing

tradeoffs: Telemetry volume is billed: sample traces and set log retention

supporting.justification: Every push runs the tests and deploys the same way; hosted runners mean no build server to operate. All 5 engineers (team.size) release through the same pipeline.

alternatives.why_not: Equivalent pipelines; one more tool to learn for no gain here

tradeoffs: Pipeline minutes are metered on hosted runners

warnings.message: Budget below the top of the estimate. The estimate is $1,190-$2,792/month against a budget of $1,500/month: the low end fits, the top end does not, and its middle ($1,991/month) is above it too. The top end is the price at ~3x today's load in the Large (5,000-50,000 users online at once) tier; the lines that grow most: Database: PostgreSQL ($600-$1,244/month); Hosting: Fly.io ($375-$845/month). Plan for the low end and watch those lines; raise the budget before the load grows, or lower the availability target or scale inputs if they were set high.

Fly.io publishes no uptime SLA. Your 99.9% target rests on the app alone: Fly.io commits to no uptime figure and owes no credit when it is down. Alert on an external uptime check and keep a fallback ready (a second region or provider); pick a host with a published SLA if the target is contractual.
